cues.text: Section three: IT service management foundations.
IT service management, or ITSM, is the structured management of IT-enabled services so that they deliver value to the business and to users.
Traditional technology management may concentrate on devices and technical components.
ITSM instead focuses on the outcomes that users actually receive.
Consider this example: a functioning database is not enough if customers cannot complete their transactions.
Next, the idea of a service.
A service combines resources and activities to facilitate desired outcomes.
Two qualities are used to judge it.
Utility means fitness for purpose, and the question it asks is whether the service does what users need.
Warranty means fitness for use, and the question it asks is whether the service is sufficiently available, secure, reliable and capable.
Now three related terms.
A service portfolio contains services across their lifecycle.
A service catalogue describes the services that are available and how users obtain them.
A service desk is a central contact point for support and communication.
Let us turn to the core practices.
First, incident management.
It restores normal service quickly.
A payment outage is an incident.
Second, problem management.
It identifies and manages underlying causes.
Repeated outages caused by a memory leak represent a problem.
Third, service request management.
It handles routine requests, such as approved software access.
Fourth, change enablement.
It assesses and authorises changes according to risk.
Fifth, service configuration management.
It maintains information about configuration items and the relationships between them.
Sixth, knowledge management.
It captures reusable troubleshooting and operational knowledge.
Finally, a distinction worth remembering.
An incident can be resolved through a workaround before its root cause is fixed.
A problem record can remain open after the incident closes.
This distinction matters in examinations, and it matters just as much in real operations.
